blocks.text: You will be an eagle in the clouds: the Scholiast on Aristophanes, Birds, says this means that they τοσοῦτον αὐξηθήσεσθαι, ὅσον αἰετὸς τῶν ἄλλων ὀρνέων ἐν ταῖς νεφέλαις προὔχει [tosouton auxēthēsesthai, hoson aietos tōn allōn orneōn en tais nephelais prouchei], will be increased as much as the eagle in the clouds stands out above the other birds. Aben Ezra too, on Iob. XXIX, 30.: אין עוף שיגבה יותר ממנו, There is no bird that rises higher. And Kimchi, on Ierem. XLIX, 16., asserts that it flies גבוה מכל העופות, higher than all birds. And Apuleius, Florida book 1: For the eagle, when it has raised itself most high, up to the clouds, borne on its wings, beyond that whole space where it rains and snows, beyond which summit there is no place for thunderbolt or lightning, in the very floor, so to speak, of the aether and the topmost height of winter. And Horus, book 2, ch. 53: ὑψηλότερον πάντων τῶν πετεινῶν ἵπταται [hypsēloteron pantōn tōn peteinōn hiptatai], it flies highest of all birds. Hence the poets call it ὑψιπετὴς [hypsipetēs] and ὑψιπετήεις [hypsipetēeis] ^{a)}, high-flying. Indeed, for this very reason, that it flies on high, if we believe Aristotle, Histor. book 9, ch. 32, θεῖον οἱ ἄνθρωποί φασιν εἶναι μόνον τῶν ὀρνέων [theion hoi anthrōpoi phasin einai monon tōn orneōn], men say it alone among birds is divine. At least from this arose the fables of the eagle in the bosom of Jupiter, and as the minister of his thunderbolts; and that some dreamed its feathers were scorched by the elemental fire, others by the rays of the nearby sun. Not to mention the eagle that used to be released from the pyre of the Caesars, as though to carry the emperor's soul to heaven. For so it was believed. Dio, book 56, on the funeral of Augustus: Καὶ ἡ πύρα μὲν ἀναλίσκετο· ἀετὸς δέ τις ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀφεθεὶς ἀπίπτατο, ὃ καὶ δὲ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἐς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀναφέρων [Kai hē pyra men anaKisketo; aetos de tis ex autēs aphetheis apeptato, ho kai de tēn psychēn autou es ton ouranon anapherōn]. And the pyre was consumed, and from it flew an eagle, bearing his soul to heaven. Herodian, book 4: Ἀετὸς ἀφίεται σὺν τῷ πυρὶ ἀνελευσόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα, ὃς φέρειν ἀπὸ γῆς ἐς οὐρανὸν τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως ψυχὴν πιστεύεται ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων [Aetos aphietai syn tō pyri aneleusomenos eis ton aithera, hos pherein apo gēs es ouranon tēn tou basileōs psychēn pisteuetai hypo Rhōmaiōn]: Together with the (kindled) fire an eagle is released to ascend into the aether, which the Romans believe carries the emperor's soul from earth to heaven. Accordingly on ancient coins one may see on one side the emperor's portrait, on the other an eagle on which the emperor sits, with this inscription: CONSECRATIO S. C. And if a king or prince dreams that he is carried by an eagle, this portends death for them, writes Artemidorus, book 2,

[II, 754] ch. 20, because there was an old custom πλάσσειν τε, καὶ γράφειν ἐπὶ ἀετῶν ὀχουμένους [plassein te, kai graphein epi aetōn ochoumenous], to sculpt and paint them seated on eagles. What of the fact that from Scripture itself it seems one can gather that the eagle flies right up to heaven and has its nest among the stars? For so Solomon, Proverb. XXIII, 5.: Like an eagle it will fly to heaven. And Obadiah, vers. 4., addressing the Edomites, proud of the height of their strongholds: Though you exalt yourself like the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, thence I will bring you down, says the Lord. But even boys know that heaven is taken by the Hebrews for the air. And the nest set among the stars is said with the same hyperbole with which the king of Babylon boasts, Esa. XIV, 13. I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God. Not unlike this is the boast of Xerxes in Herodotus, book 7, ch. 10: Γῆν τε τὴν Περσίδα ἀποδέξομεν τῷ Διὸς αἰθέρι ὁμουρέουσαν [Gēn te tēn Persida apodexomen tō Dios aitheri homoureousan], We shall make the Persian land border on the aether of Jupiter. That is, just as exalting one's throne above the stars and making one's land border on the aether of Jupiter means raising it to the highest summit of loftiness, so one who nests in the loftiest places is said to set his nest among the stars. That the eagle does this, besides Obadiah, Jeremiah also teaches in a passage parallel to this, addressed to the same Edomites, Ier. XLIX, 16.: O you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who [col. 173] hold the summit of the hill. Though you should make your nest as high as the eagle, thence I would bring you down. And there the Chaldee paraphrast: You are like the eagle, which lives בשני כיפא, on the crags of the rock: its dwelling is בתקוף רומא, in a lofty stronghold.
